title: Robot Decomposition Tree
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: Split a big robot goal such as "Avoid the wall" into smaller tasks, and keep splitting until every piece is small enough to write as a line or two of MicroPython.

educational.topic: Decomposition of robot goals into codable sub-tasks
learningObjectives: Break a robot goal into two or three smaller sub-tasks
Keep splitting sub-tasks until each one is small enough to write as code
Recognize when a task still hides more than one action
Connect each finished piece to a one-line MicroPython idea
prerequisites: The four pillars of computational thinking (Chapter 1: What Is Computational Thinking?)
The three-task breakdown of avoiding a wall (Chapter 1: Decomposition)

controls.label: Tree box
controls.purpose: Select a task in the tree

controls.label: Split it
controls.purpose: Break the selected task into smaller tasks

controls.label: Small enough to code?
controls.purpose: Mark the selected task green if it is ready to code

controls.label: Reset
controls.purpose: Return to the single goal node

simulationModel.modelType: Fixed answer-bank tree that grows on demand
assumptions: Each goal has one agreed decomposition in the answer bank
A task with no further sub-tasks in the bank is small enough to code
limitations: Real problems can be decomposed in more than one correct way
Code ideas are short sketches, not complete runnable programs

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Guided practice with immediate feedback on the stopping rule
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Click-to-select tree builder with Split and Check buttons
keyQuestions: How do you know when a task is small enough to code?
Why is 'If distance is under 20 cm, stop and turn' still too big?
Which pieces of 'Follow a line' also appear in 'Avoid the wall'?
How many green pieces does a full decomposition of 'Avoid the wall' have?
commonMisconceptions: A task that fits in one sentence is automatically small enough to code
Decomposition means writing the whole program in one long list
There is only one correct way to decompose a problem
assessmentOpportunities: Challenge answer: 5 green pieces, using decomposition
Compare a paper decomposition with the MicroSim's answer bank
Exit ticket: two-level tree for a new robot goal with codable leaves circled
